evidence.title: Entropy Production of Hydrate Transport in Subsea Multiphase Pipeline Flows
evidence.abstract: A numerical model is developed to examine the flow conditions of multiphase heat transfer and entropy production during hydrate formation in subsea pipelines. The temperature and pressure gradients of the oil and gas flow in subsea pipelines lead to entropy generation. This paper examines the impacts and effects of thermodynamic irreversibilities on the nucleation and growth processes of hydrate crystals in the pipeline flows. The effects of heat transfer ratio, internal diameter of the pipe, molar gas density, and environment temperature on entropy production in subsea pipelines are predicted and discussed in this paper. The numerical model accounts for the temperature distribution along the axial length of the pipe, reaction kinetics, and mass transfer between the solid and fluid layer. The kinetic energy of the hydrate particles during the coagulation process is analyzed in the numerical model. The results indicate that entropy production is highest at the beginning of the nucleation process. Pipelines with smaller internal radii have a lower rate of hydrate formation in subsea pipelines. The results from the numerical model are verified by comparison with experimental results for structure type II natural gas hydrates

evidence.title: Characterization of Restart Pressure in Production Pipeline for Waxy Crude Oil as A Result of Injection of Non-Reacting Gas
evidence.abstract: Wax deposition within the walls of production pipeline of crude oil causes flow assurance issue due to reduction in flow rate. In the event of planned maintenance or an emergency shutdown due to bad weather condition, the crude oil will stop flowing in the pipeline, in which the temperature of the crude oil may drop below the Pour Point Temperature (PPT). As the crude oil is under a quiescent condition, wax crude oil may precipitate out of its liquid phase and becomes a wax-gel oil like substance, which may cause blockage in the pipeline. A high pumping pressure is needed in order to restart the pipeline and disintegrate the wax-oil gel. A recent study on gas voids in cured oil showed that the presence of gas voids within the pipeline could reduce the restart pressure needed to restart a crude oil production pipeline. It was anticipated that the volume of the gas voids could be increased through the injection of non-reacting gas in order to reduce the restart pressure needed. However, there was no previous attempt to study if the proposal would be practical in practice. The present study is aimed at studying the effects and effectiveness of gas bubbles intrusion through injection of external gas with respect to the restart pressure. A waxy crude oil flow loop was used in order to simulate the condition of a gelled waxy crude oil within the crude oil production line

evidence.title:
Investigation of Hydrate Agglomeration and Plugging
Mechanism in Low-Wax-Content Water-in-Oil Emulsion Systems
evidence.abstract:
Pipeline
blockage caused by hydrates and wax in subsea pipelines is a major
hazard for flow assurance in the petroleum industry. When hydrates
and wax coexist in a flow system, the plugging risk is more severe.
The effects of wax on hydrate formation, agglomeration process, flow
properties, and plugging mechanisms were studied in a high-pressure
flow loop using water-in-oil (w/o) emulsion systems. The flow properties
of the system with the presence of wax were entirely different from
those of the system without wax under the same experimental conditions.
Three types of plugging were observed in the flow loop: rapid plugging,
transition plugging, and gradual plugging. The interaction relationships
between wax crystals, water droplets, and hydrate particles and the
formation of wax–hydrate aggregates were proposed based on
the particle video measurement (PVM) probe observation and the analysis
of the fluid viscosity. The mechanisms of different plugging scenarios
were presented, which were highly correlated with the temperature
and initial flow rate. The presence of wax would impact on the agglomeration
process of hydrate particles leading to a catastrophic decrease in
the transportation ability and an extremely high plugging risk after
hydrate formation in the pipeline

evidence.title: Transient Wax Gel Formation Model for Shut-In Subsea Pipelines
evidence.abstract: Physics of wax gel formation during shut-in is analyzed and described over a cross-section of a typical subsea pipeline. Two regions are identified during this process: the liquid and gel regions. Phase transition is assumed to occur at the liquid-gel interface. Unsteady-state heat and mass transfer models are proposed for each region. Two diffusion streams are evaluated: the dissolved wax molecules moving from the pipe center toward the wall due to temperature gradient and subsequently concentration gradient and the wax molecules diffusing from the liquid-gel interface into the gel deposit. This model is essentially the modification of the model given by Bhat et al. [1] which considered transient heat transfer and neglected mass transfer of wax molecules through the gel deposit and the model by Singh et al. [2] which considered transient mass transfer of molecules with carbon numbers higher than the` critical carbon number (CCN) necessary for wax diffusion into gel deposit but did not consider transient heat transfer effects during the cooling process. This paper presents a transient-state formulation circumventing the limitations of these previous models and better represents the true cooling and gelation process occurring in a shut-in subsea pipeline filled with waxy crude.</jats:p

evidence.title: Wax removal using pipeline pigs
evidence.abstract: The deposition of paraffin wax solids in pipelines and risers represents a continuing challenge to flow assurance in offshore installations. Wax deposits reduce product throughput, requiring increased energy expenditure to re-establish flow levels. In severe cases, wax deposits can completely block a pipeline. Preventative solutions to the problem such as pipeline insulation, active heating of pipes or chemical dosing with wax inhibitors are not always economically viable, so mechanical removal using a device known as a 'pig' remains an economical solution to the problem of wax removal. A pig is a cylindrical tool that is driven through the pipe by the flow of product, scraping deposits from the pipe wall as it travels. Despite the importance of pipeline pigging to the oil and gas industry, the effectiveness of pigs in removing wax is poorly understood and it is this problem that is addressed by this thesis. One of the first necessities in undertaking this work has been to define the mechanical properties of wax deposits. This has required critical analysis of published material on the subject of wax deposition along with practical experimentation to create representative models of wax deposits that require mechanical removal from pipelines. Previously, studies of wax removal using pigs have assumed the mechanics of the process to be adequately represented by uniaxial compression or simple shear load models. In this work wax removal is analysed using the orthogonal cutting model. This provides a more accurate description of the process as it includes the effect of material after yielding (the chip) on the net wax removal force. Experiments were designed to allow testing of the validity of the orthogonal cutting theory to the pigging process under a variety of conditions. An original contribution from this work is through experimental and theoretical results that are given context through comparison with established metal cutting theory. Through experimentation a specific cutting energy is obtained for wax removal. informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: A numerical model is developed to examine the flow conditions of multiphase heat transfer and entropy production during hydrate formation in subsea pipelines. The temperature and pressure gradients of the oil and gas flow in subsea pipelines lead to entropy generation. This paper examines the impacts and effects of thermodynamic irreversibilities on the nucleation and growth processes of hydrate crystals in the pipeline flows. The effects of heat transfer ratio, internal diameter of the pipe, molar gas density, and environment temperature on entropy production in subsea pipelines are predicted and discussed in this paper. The numerical model accounts for the temperature distribution along the axial length of the pipe, reaction kinetics, and mass transfer between the solid and fluid layer. The kinetic energy of the hydrate particles during the coagulation process is analyzed in the numerical model. The results indicate that entropy production is highest at the beginning of the nucleation process. Pipelines with smaller internal radii have a lower rate of hydrate formation in subsea pipelines. The results from the numerical model are verified by comparison with experimental results for structure type II natural gas hydrates

custody_records.raw_content: Wax deposition within the walls of production pipeline of crude oil causes flow assurance issue due to reduction in flow rate. In the event of planned maintenance or an emergency shutdown due to bad weather condition, the crude oil will stop flowing in the pipeline, in which the temperature of the crude oil may drop below the Pour Point Temperature (PPT). As the crude oil is under a quiescent condition, wax crude oil may precipitate out of its liquid phase and becomes a wax-gel oil like substance, which may cause blockage in the pipeline. A high pumping pressure is needed in order to restart the pipeline and disintegrate the wax-oil gel. A recent study on gas voids in cured oil showed that the presence of gas voids within the pipeline could reduce the restart pressure needed to restart a crude oil production pipeline. It was anticipated that the volume of the gas voids could be increased through the injection of non-reacting gas in order to reduce the restart pressure needed. However, there was no previous attempt to study if the proposal would be practical in practice. The present study is aimed at studying the effects and effectiveness of gas bubbles intrusion through injection of external gas with respect to the restart pressure. A waxy crude oil flow loop was used in order to simulate the condition of a gelled waxy crude oil within the crude oil production line

blockage caused by hydrates and wax in subsea pipelines is a major
hazard for flow assurance in the petroleum industry. When hydrates
and wax coexist in a flow system, the plugging risk is more severe.
The effects of wax on hydrate formation, agglomeration process, flow
properties, and plugging mechanisms were studied in a high-pressure
flow loop using water-in-oil (w/o) emulsion systems. The flow properties
of the system with the presence of wax were entirely different from
those of the system without wax under the same experimental conditions.
Three types of plugging were observed in the flow loop: rapid plugging,
transition plugging, and gradual plugging. The interaction relationships
between wax crystals, water droplets, and hydrate particles and the
formation of wax–hydrate aggregates were proposed based on
the particle video measurement (PVM) probe observation and the analysis
of the fluid viscosity. The mechanisms of different plugging scenarios
were presented, which were highly correlated with the temperature
and initial flow rate. The presence of wax would impact on the agglomeration
process of hydrate particles leading to a catastrophic decrease in
the transportation ability and an extremely high plugging risk after
hydrate formation in the pipeline

custody_records.raw_content: Physics of wax gel formation during shut-in is analyzed and described over a cross-section of a typical subsea pipeline. Two regions are identified during this process: the liquid and gel regions. Phase transition is assumed to occur at the liquid-gel interface. Unsteady-state heat and mass transfer models are proposed for each region. Two diffusion streams are evaluated: the dissolved wax molecules moving from the pipe center toward the wall due to temperature gradient and subsequently concentration gradient and the wax molecules diffusing from the liquid-gel interface into the gel deposit. This model is essentially the modification of the model given by Bhat et al. [1] which considered transient heat transfer and neglected mass transfer of wax molecules through the gel deposit and the model by Singh et al. [2] which considered transient mass transfer of molecules with carbon numbers higher than the` critical carbon number (CCN) necessary for wax diffusion into gel deposit but did not consider transient heat transfer effects during the cooling process. This paper presents a transient-state formulation circumventing the limitations of these previous models and better represents the true cooling and gelation process occurring in a shut-in subsea pipeline filled with waxy crude.</jats:p

custody_records.raw_content: The deposition of paraffin wax solids in pipelines and risers represents a continuing challenge to flow assurance in offshore installations. A pig is a cylindrical tool that is driven through the pipe by the flow of product, scraping deposits from the pipe wall as it travels. Despite the importance of pipeline pigging to the oil and gas industry, the effectiveness of pigs in removing wax is poorly understood and it is this problem that is addressed by this thesis. One of the first necessities in undertaking this work has been to define the mechanical properties of wax deposits. This has required critical analysis of published material on the subject of wax deposition along with practical experimentation to create representative models of wax deposits that require mechanical removal from pipelines. Previously, studies of wax removal using pigs have assumed the mechanics of the process to be adequately represented by uniaxial compression or simple shear load models. In this work wax removal is analysed using the orthogonal cutting model. This provides a more accurate description of the process as it includes the effect of material after yielding (the chip) on the net wax removal force. Experiments were designed to allow testing of the validity of the orthogonal cutting theory to the pigging process under a variety of conditions.
